narrationScript: While Moore's Law continued, Dennard scaling eventually reached its limits around 2005. As transistors shrunk to atomic scales, a phenomenon called leakage current became significant. This meant that even when a transistor was 'off,' a small amount of current would still leak through, generating heat. Consequently, power density started to *increase* with shrinking transistors, rather than staying constant. This created what we call the 'power wall.' Processors could no longer be scaled to higher frequencies without generating excessive heat and exceeding thermal limits. A prime example was the Intel Pentium 4, which pushed clock frequencies to nearly 4 GHz but consumed over 100 watts and was notoriously difficult to cool. Recognizing this fundamental physical limitation, the industry made a pivotal shift. Instead of trying to make a single core run faster, architects turned to 'multicore scaling,' placing multiple, often simpler, processor cores on the same chip. This allowed for parallel execution, performing more work simultaneously even if individual cores weren't dramatically faster. This new paradigm introduced further concepts like 'dark silicon,' where, even with billions of transistors, not all of them can be powered on simultaneously due to thermal constraints. Parts of the chip must remain 'dark' or inactive. It also spurred the rise of 'heterogeneous computing,' where chips combine different types of cores, such as 'big' high-performance cores and 'little' energy-efficient cores, to balance power and performance. Furthermore, the need for specialized processing led to dedicated 'accelerators' like Graphics Processing Units, or GPUs, and Neural Processing Units, NPUs, for tasks like AI and machine learning. These architectural innovations became the new path for performance gains in a post-Dennard scaling world.
